titulo.texto: Mixtec Gold Pectorals and the Treasure of Tomb 7

frase_gancho.texto: The gold of a Mixtec lord, buried in a tomb that was not his own.

puente_narrativo.texto: Gold was not the only luxury in that tomb. Now look for a human skull covered with hundreds of tiny pieces of turquoise, gazing at you with eyes of shell.

guion_corto.texto: In the goldwork display cases of this hall, you will see the gleaming gold of the Mixtec lords of Oaxaca, such as the pectorals and necklaces found at Zaachila and Yanhuitlán. They were heirs to the same tradition that produced the famous Great Pectoral of Tomb 7 at Monte Albán. Discovered by Alfonso Caso in January 1932, Tomb 7 revealed more than five hundred objects of gold, silver, turquoise and rock crystal, which today are kept in the Museum of the Cultures of Oaxaca, with samples and reproductions here in Chapultepec. These jewels were cast by the lost-wax method, with plates joined by movable rings and bells along the lower edge that jingled with every step of the ruler.

guion_largo.texto:
On January 9, 1932, the archaeologist Alfonso Caso and his team opened a tomb at Monte Albán and came upon something no one expected: gold. A great deal of gold. Necklaces, ear ornaments, pectorals, vessels of crystal and alabaster, carved bones, a [skull with turquoise](mna_s07_craneo_turquesa): more than five hundred objects. It was one of the most important finds in Mexican archaeology, and its pieces are still being studied.

The curious thing is that the tomb was not Mixtec. The Zapotec had built it many centuries earlier, when Monte Albán was still a great city, like the [Tomb 104](mna_s07_tumba_104) you have just seen. The Mixtec reopened it, much later, and buried a person of very high rank there. Perhaps they wanted to claim the prestige of the ancient lords: being buried in a Zapotec tomb was like being buried in a historic building.

In the great Mixtec pectorals, both those from Zaachila displayed in this hall and the celebrated pectoral of Tomb 7, the jewel is formed by several plates joined by rings, so that the piece moved with the person wearing it. At the top appears a figure with a great feathered headdress; specialists debate whether it is a ruler or a deity. And from the lower part hang bells. Imagine the effect: each step of the lord produced a metallic sound, as if a small wind were walking with him.

How was it made? With the technique called lost wax. First the piece was modeled in wax, with all its details; then it was covered with clay, leaving an opening; it was heated so that the wax melted and ran out, and through that hole the molten gold was poured. When the mold was broken, the jewel appeared. That is why each piece was unique: the mold was destroyed at the end.

The Mixtec knew that gold was sacred. For them, and also for the Mexica, it was the material of the gods and of the Sun. The Mexica called it teocuitlatl, which is usually translated as «excrement of the gods». It sounds strange today, but it was a compliment: something the gods leave on the earth and that shines like the Sun. It was used for insignia and offerings, not as money; to trade, people used cacao beans or cotton cloaks.

Metallurgy arrived late in Mesoamerica. It is thought to have come from South America, along the Pacific coast, around the year seven hundred, and to have been practiced first in West Mexico. In the West Hall you will see bells and a [copper pectoral](mna_s10_cobre_purepecha) worked by the Purépecha. But it was the Mixtec who brought gold to its greatest beauty. It is said that the Mexica hired Mixtec artisans for their workshops, because they were the best.

The Mixtec called themselves Ñuu Savi, «people of the rain», and the Zapotec called themselves «people of the clouds». Two mountain peoples, defined by water. The Mixtec also painted books, the codices, which tell of genealogies and wars. One of them, the Codex Vindobonensis, is in Vienna, the same city that keeps the [feather headdress](mna_s06_penacho_moctezuma). Vienna holds two great treasures of Mexico.

Today, most of the treasure of Tomb 7 is on display in Oaxaca, in the Museum of the Cultures, in the former convent of Santo Domingo. If you go someday, you will see the whole tomb brought together: the gold, the turquoise, the crystal. Here you have a sample, and an invitation to continue the journey.

texto: Look in the display case at the gold plates joined by movable rings and the tiny bells along the lower edge
Look for the faces of rulers or solar deities with filigree headdresses
Notice the very fine gold threads that imitate feathers and step-fret patterns

texto.Material: Gold cast by the lost-wax method, with false filigree and bells
texto.Origin: Zaachila, Yanhuitlán and Tomb 7 of Monte Albán, Oaxaca (discovered by Alfonso Caso, January 9, 1932; the main group from Tomb 7 is kept in the Museum of the Cultures of Oaxaca)

texto.pregunta: Myth: The ancient Mexicans used gold as money.
texto.respuesta: Reality: Gold was a sacred material, a symbol of the Sun and the gods, reserved for lords and priests. For trade, people used cacao beans, cotton cloaks and other goods.
